ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & Thickness Gauging | Indianapolis, IN
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and weld UT for Indianapolis plants, fabricators, tank farms and bridge steel, with Level III review. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) and Thickness Inspection in Indianapolis, Indiana
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes ultrasonic technicians to Indianapolis plants, fabrication shops, storage tank farms, process facilities and steel structures to measure wall thickness and examine welds in carbon and low-alloy steel. Typical scopes are pressure vessel and piping corrosion surveys, tank shell and floor thickness checks, plate lamination checks, and shear-wave examination of structural and pressure welds. Request a UT quote for your Indianapolis site with the asset list, drawings and code, and we respond within one business day.

Where ultrasonic testing is used in Indianapolis

Indianapolis has been a metalworking city since the days of its early iron foundries and rolling mills, and the region still builds engines, transmissions, axles and other heavy mechanical products. Rolls-Royce operates a large defense engine campus in the city, and transmission, truck and automotive suppliers fill the surrounding counties. Their plants run boilers, air systems, hydraulic equipment and process piping, and their fabricators weld frames, housings and pressure parts. Pharmaceutical and food manufacturing add stainless process piping and steam systems to the mix.

Indiana is also a grain and fuel state. Ethanol and grain-processing plants, petroleum product terminals and propane facilities use large storage tanks, and the interstate corridors that cross at Indianapolis carry steel bridges that the state and cities inspect and repair. UT is the method that answers the question these assets share: how much metal is left, and are the welds sound?

  • Manufacturing plants: boiler and steam piping, compressed air receivers, process vessels, heat exchangers
  • Tank farms and terminals: shell courses, bottoms and nozzle neck thickness on atmospheric tanks
  • Fabrication shops: plate lamination checks, production weld examination on frames and pressure parts
  • Bridges and structures: groove welds and plate thickness on steel girders and connections under bridge and structural welding codes

What UT finds, and what it misses

An ultrasonic probe sends a short pulse of sound into steel and listens for echoes. The time between pulse and back-wall echo converts to thickness, which is why UT is the standard tool for corrosion surveys. An echo that arrives early, from inside the wall, reveals a lamination, crack, slag line or lack of fusion. Because the sound travels through the full thickness, UT sees internal planar flaws that surface methods cannot.

The method has limits that a competent procedure plans around. Rough, scaled or heavily pitted surfaces scatter the sound and must be dressed. Coarse-grained castings and some stainless welds attenuate the beam. Very thin plate produces multiple echoes that can fool a digital gauge. Flaws oriented along the beam, and flaws in the shallow dead zone just under the probe face, may escape a single scan, so the procedure uses more than one angle or probe when a particular flaw is a concern.

How thickness gauging is done on Indiana equipment

The technician starts by calibrating on a step block made of the same material as the component, covering the range of thickness to be read. For corroded or rough surfaces, a dual-element probe is used because its two crystals work around surface irregularities and give a stable reading on pitted metal. The display is observed as an A-scan, so a laminated plate or a doubled echo is recognized instead of being recorded as a false thickness.

On tanks, readings are taken at marked locations on every shell course, and bottoms are checked where the lower courses meet the floor and along critical zones. On pressure vessels and piping, condition monitoring locations are marked so they can be read again in the next campaign, and the corrosion rate then comes from two measured thicknesses rather than a guess. Hot lines need a high-temperature probe and couplant with a velocity correction.

Cold weather matters here. Couplant gel thickens and can freeze on a winter morning in Indiana, so a low-temperature couplant or a warmed bottle is used and the calibration is checked on a block at working temperature.

Weld examination with angle beams

For welds, the technician selects shear-wave angle probes, commonly 45, 60 and 70 degrees, to hit the weld bevel and the heat-affected zone. A reference level or distance-amplitude curve is built on a block containing side-drilled holes. The scan covers the weld from both sides where possible, and each indication is located, sized and compared with the acceptance rules. UT handles lack of fusion, cracks and slag in thicker welds well, and it is written into AWS D1.1 for groove welds, into ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 12, and into provisions of ASME B31.3 and API 1104. A written scan plan and recorded amplitudes form the record, since UT does not produce a picture the way film does.

Tanks, terminals, and grain and ethanol plants

Storage tanks are among the most common ultrasonic jobs in Indiana. Ethanol and grain plants hold liquids in vertical tanks, fuel terminals around the metro area store gasoline and diesel, and plants keep water, chemical and oil tanks of every size. Under API 653 the owner's authorized inspector decides on repair and interval; our part is the thickness evidence. Technicians take a set of readings on each shell course, usually along vertical lines, and examine the first course and the floor-to-shell junction more closely because those are the places where corrosion concentrates. Tank bottoms are scanned for loss from the soil side only where a procedure and equipment suitable for the job are agreed, so the quote states exactly what will be covered and what will not.

Roof structures, nozzle necks, manways and attached piping are checked too, and the readings are recorded against a tank diagram so the next inspection can compare them point by point.

Bridge steel, structures and fabrication shops

Indiana's highway network crosses at Indianapolis, and the steel bridges that carry those routes are inspected and repaired under state transportation department specifications that build on AWS D1.5. Ultrasonic examination of groove welds and thickness checks on plates and flanges are part of that work. Building steel follows AWS D1.1, where ultrasonic examination of groove welds is one of the permitted methods. In fabrication shops, plates are checked for laminations before cutting, particularly when they will carry through-thickness loads, and production welds on pressure parts or equipment frames are scanned while rework is still easy. Reports give the owner or engineer a record that is easy to attach to a quality data book.

Codes and acceptance criteria for Indianapolis work

Methods follow ASME Section V: Article 4 for welds, Article 5 for materials and Article 23 with SE-797 for contact thickness. Acceptance is taken from the governing code: ASME Section VIII Division 1 for vessels, B31.3 for process piping, B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for bridges. In-service equipment follows API 510 for vessels, API 570 for piping and API 653 for tanks, where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection and Atlantis performs the UT and reports thickness and indication data. ASTM E797 covers thickness measurement, E164 covers weld examination, and E114 covers straight-beam work. The contract states the edition.

Indiana pressure equipment rules

Boilers and pressure vessels in Indiana are regulated by the Boilers and Pressure Vessels Section of the Indiana Department of Homeland Security, under the Indiana Boiler and Pressure Vessel Rules in 675 IAC 30. An operating permit is needed to run a regulated unit, the permit inspection is carried out by an Indiana-licensed inspector, and each unit has a state registration number. UT data feeds those inspections and repair records. Indiana also runs its own workplace safety plan through the Indiana Department of Labor, and site rules on confined spaces, fall protection and lockout apply to technicians the same as to employees. Where a plant is covered by OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j) calls for mechanical integrity inspections that follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practice.

Who performs the work

Our UT personnel are qualified through a written practice that follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II personnel calibrate, scan and interpret; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. The employer issues the qualifications under SNT-TC-1A. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. If your site requires technicians qualified to a different scheme, say so when you request the quote.

What the UT report contains

The report names the component and drawing, the procedure and revision, the instrument and probe, the calibration block and the calibration check, the technician and level, and the surface condition. Thickness reports give a table of readings by location with nominal thickness, minimum required thickness and any reading below the retirement limit. Weld reports give the scan plan, reference level, scanning gain, every reportable indication with location, length and amplitude, and a code-based accept or reject decision. Marking sketches and photographs let the next campaign repeat the same points.

Planning a UT job in Indianapolis

Technicians travel to your site, so planning centers on access, season and schedule. Indianapolis winters are cold enough to stiffen couplant, slow batteries and leave steel coated with frost, and summers are hot and humid, so exposed tank shells can be uncomfortable and hot to the touch. Spring brings storms and tornado warnings that stop scaffold and tank work on short notice. Plant outages and tank cleanings are scheduled well ahead, and fabricators work to their delivery dates, so book early. We do not keep an office in Indianapolis, and quotes include travel to the site, orientation time and access equipment such as scaffolding or lifts.

UT, MT or PT for your Indianapolis job

Pick ultrasonic testing for thickness and for volumetric weld questions. Pick magnetic particle inspection in Indianapolis for surface cracks in steel parts, forgings and welds, and liquid penetrant testing in Indianapolis for aluminum, stainless and other non-magnetic surfaces. Many jobs pair UT with MT or PT at a repair. For statewide scope, see our NDT inspection services in Indiana hub, the national ultrasonic testing page and the Article 5 thickness measurement explainer.

Training your own UT technicians

If your plant wants its own qualified technicians, Atlantis teaches UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, and trainees can rehearse scanning on the UT practical simulator. The Indianapolis NDT training page covers local detail. Your company certifies its own personnel through its written practice.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have a shop or office in Indianapolis for UT?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Indianapolis. Level II technicians travel to your site with the instruments, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report under a written practice built on SNT-TC-1A.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing measure on a storage tank?
faq.a: It measures remaining wall on shell courses, bottoms and nozzle necks at marked locations. Comparing readings over time shows the corrosion rate and helps the owner and inspector decide when repair or retirement is needed.

faq.q: Can UT be done on a hot or very cold surface in Indiana?
faq.a: Yes, with the right setup. Hot lines need a high-temperature probe and couplant with a velocity correction, while winter work needs low-temperature couplant and calibration at working temperature.

faq.q: Which codes cover UT weld inspection for Indianapolis fabricators?
faq.a: Method rules are in ASME Section V Article 4, and acceptance comes from the construction code, such as ASME Section VIII, B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 for buildings or AWS D1.5 for bridges.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic examination substitute for radiography on a weld?
faq.a: Only where the code and the owner allow it. Section VIII, B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 each treat UT differently, so agree the change with the engineer and inspector before work starts.

faq.q: What surface condition does UT need?
faq.a: The scan surface must be free of loose scale, spatter and flaking coating so the probe couples. Weld caps may need grinding flat for angle-beam work, and the procedure states what is required.

faq.q: Who is responsible for inspection decisions on API 510, 570 or 653 equipment?
faq.a: The owner's authorized inspector. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work, records the thickness and indication data, and reports it, while the inspector applies the code to decide fitness and next inspection dates.

faq.q: What should I send to get a UT quote for Indianapolis?
faq.a: Send drawings or tank and vessel data sheets, material and nominal thickness, the code and edition, access details, any existing monitoring location list and your target dates.

faq.q: Can Atlantis train my maintenance staff in UT?
faq.a: Yes. Courses cover UT Level 1 and Level 2, with a practical simulator for scanning practice. Your company then qualifies and certifies its own staff under its written practice, as SNT-TC-1A requires.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection Indiana | Indianapolis MT
mt.description: On-site magnetic particle inspection in Indiana: MPI of forgings, castings, welds and heavy equipment in Indianapolis. Request an MT quote.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Indianapolis, Indiana
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes magnetic particle inspectors to Indianapolis plants, foundries, forge shops, fabricators and equipment yards, and to other Indiana sites, to find surface and near-surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel and in iron castings. Common scopes are crankshafts, gears and shafts, forgings, steel and ductile iron castings, welded frames and lifting equipment. Request an MT quote for your Indianapolis work, with the parts, material and acceptance code, and we answer within one business day.

Where magnetic particle inspection is used in Indianapolis and Indiana

Indiana makes things from steel. Indianapolis grew around foundries and machine shops, then around automobile and engine manufacturing, and the region today still produces engines, transmissions, axles, drive components and heavy equipment. Rolls-Royce builds defense engines in the city, and truck and automotive suppliers machine shafts, gears and housings nearby. Mills and service centers across the state, including the steel works in the northwest corner, feed a long chain of forges, foundries and fabricators.

Those parts are ideal for magnetic particle inspection. A crankshaft journal, a gear tooth root or a forged flange fails by fatigue cracking that starts at the surface, and MPI is the method that finds it. A welded frame for a truck, a crane or a piece of mobile equipment needs its welds checked for toe cracks and lack of fusion. Cast ductile iron and cast steel components show shrinkage, laps and surface cracks under particles.

  • Engine and drivetrain parts: crankshafts, connecting rods, camshafts, gears, axle shafts and couplings
  • Forgings and castings: flanges, hubs, housings, yokes, steel and ductile iron castings
  • Welded frames and structures: truck and trailer frames, crane booms, equipment bases, bridge and building steel
  • Lifting and rigging: hooks, lugs, pins, shackles and below-the-hook attachments

The same work is available statewide through our NDT inspection services in Indiana page, and customers searching for magnetic particle inspection in Indiana often have sites outside Indianapolis as well.

What MT finds, and what it cannot

Magnetic particle testing works only on ferromagnetic material: carbon and low-alloy steels, martensitic stainless steels and cast iron. The part is magnetized, iron particles are applied, and a surface or near-surface crack that interrupts the field attracts them into a visible line. The method is quick, inexpensive in materials and very good at tight fatigue cracks and grinding cracks.

It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper alloys or titanium, which are not magnetic. It cannot measure crack depth. Deep internal flaws are beyond its reach, and thick coatings or plating reduce sensitivity. Aluminum transmission housings, a common Indianapolis product, are therefore a penetrant job rather than a magnetic particle one.

Choosing the technique

The procedure states how the part is magnetized and what particles are used. A yoke is the usual field tool for welds and large parts, prods or cables suit heavy sections, and coils or central conductors suit shafts and rings that can be placed on the equipment. A customer's wet horizontal bench is used when one is available at the plant and the procedure specifies it, since the bench gives uniform circular and longitudinal fields on small parts. AC magnetization favors surface flaws, and DC or half-wave current reaches deeper.

Wet fluorescent particles examined under UV-A light in a dark area give the highest sensitivity, and they are the normal choice for critical machined parts. Wet visible particles on contrast paint work in daylight. Dry powder suits rough or warm surfaces. ASME Section V Article 7 requires that an AC yoke lift at least 10 pounds, and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, at the maximum pole spacing in use. Two examinations at roughly right angles ensure that cracks in any direction are found.

Codes and acceptance criteria

The method comes from ASME Section V Article 7, ASTM E1444 and the guide in ASTM E709. Acceptance is taken from the code that governs the item: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 for vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 for process piping, B31.1 for power piping, AWS D1.1 for structural steel and AWS D1.5 for bridge steel, or a customer specification for machined components. In-service pressure equipment under API 510, API 570 or API 653 is the responsibility of the owner's authorized inspector, and Atlantis carries out the MT and reports the indications. The contract states which edition applies.

Indiana rules that touch MT work

The Indiana Department of Homeland Security regulates boilers and pressure vessels under 675 IAC 30, with operating permits and Indiana-licensed inspectors. MT on a repair weld becomes part of the record the inspector reviews. The state operates its own workplace safety plan through the Indiana Department of Labor, so rules on crane inspections, lockout, confined spaces and electrical hazards around magnetizing equipment are enforced by the state. Bridge steel on public work in Indiana falls under the Indiana Department of Transportation and its specifications, which build on the AWS bridge welding code.

Lifting equipment and magnets

Some customers search for a magnet inspection service when what they own is a lifting magnet. Inspection of lifting magnets is governed by ASME B30.20 and belongs to the owner's designated person. It is different from MT. Magnetic particle testing is used on the hook, lug, pin and structure of a lifting device, for example during the inspections ASME B30.10 calls for on hooks. Atlantis performs MT; it does not rate or approve lifting equipment.

Surface preparation and reading indications

Parts are cleaned of oil, scale, paint and metal spatter before testing. Machined surfaces are usually ready as they come; as-welded or as-cast surfaces may need local grinding or blasting so that particles can move freely. The technician separates relevant indications, which come from discontinuities, from non-relevant ones, such as magnetic writing, sharp section changes or gear tooth profiles. A suspected crack is re-examined after conditioning. Linear indications, with length more than three times width, are measured and compared with the acceptance table, and rounded indications are judged separately.

Examining machined parts and shafts

For crankshafts, gear blanks, rings and other machined parts, the strongest set-up is a wet horizontal bench with circular and longitudinal magnetization, and where a plant owns one, the procedure can specify it. Without a bench, a portable coil or yoke is used. Journals, keyways, fillets and gear roots get special attention since fatigue starts at stress raisers. The procedure states the current, the number of shots, and the dwell time of the bath, and it sets the particle concentration, which is checked with a centrifuge tube before use. Parts that are ground after heat treatment are especially prone to grinding cracks, which appear as a fine network or as parallel lines at right angles to the grinding direction.

Heavy equipment, welded frames and lifting gear

Welded frames, booms and bases on trucks, cranes and mobile equipment concentrate stress at weld toes and at the ends of gussets, and those are the places inspectors look first. Indianapolis maintenance shops and fabricators that build or repair such structures use MT to check fit-up root passes, completed welds and weld repairs. Pins, lugs and hooks on lifting equipment are examined for cracks at the load-bearing surfaces. The inspector records each location against a sketch or photograph so that the repairs can be checked off after rework and the area re-examined.

Equipment checks and field safety

Before a job, the yoke is checked with a calibrated lifting weight, the UV and white light meters are confirmed to be in date, and bath concentration is tested. Cables, plugs and ground-fault protection are inspected. Prods are energized only after contact is made, since arcing burns the work surface and can create new cracks. At heights, in confined spaces and around live equipment, the site safety plan governs, and technicians take the plant's orientation before starting work.

Who does the work

MT is carried out by Level II technicians qualified under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. An ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews records, and Anoop Rayavarapu holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer issues the qualification. Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification.

What the MT report contains

A report lists the component, drawing and location, the procedure and revision, the equipment and its calibration status, the yoke lift check, particle type and concentration, UV intensity and ambient light level for fluorescent work, surface condition, and technician and level. Every indication is recorded with location, length and orientation, accepted or rejected against the named code, and photographed where possible. If demagnetization is required, the report records the residual field check afterward, because magnetism left in a crankshaft or gear can attract chips into bearings.

Planning an MT job in Indianapolis

Technicians travel to your site with portable equipment. Indianapolis winters are cold enough that wet particle suspensions thicken and parts arrive from outdoor storage coated in frost, so work areas need to be heated or the parts brought inside; the carrier fluid and surface must be checked against the procedure temperature. Summer humidity and heat shorten drying times and degrade dry powder. Fluorescent work needs a dark area, which in a busy plant means a booth or a tent. Plant shutdowns and tooling changeovers are scheduled early, so book dates when you plan the outage. We have no office in Indianapolis; the quote reflects travel and orientation time.

MT, PT or UT for your Indianapolis job

For steel and iron parts, MT is generally the faster and more sensitive way to find surface cracks. Choose dye penetrant inspection in Indianapolis for aluminum housings, stainless steel and other non-magnetic material, and ultrasonic testing in Indianapolis when thickness or internal weld condition matters. Our guides on magnetic particle testing, MT versus PT and Article 7 requirements go into more detail, and the national magnetic particle testing page covers the service.

Training your own MT technicians

Plants that would rather build in-house capability can begin with MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and see the Indianapolis NDT training page for local details. Your company certifies its own technicians under its written practice.

faq.q: What parts can magnetic particle inspection check in Indiana?
faq.a: Any ferromagnetic part: crankshafts, gears, shafts, forgings, steel and ductile iron castings, welded frames, hooks and lugs. It finds surface and near-surface cracks that fatigue or welding can create.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in Indianapolis for MPI?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Indianapolis. Qualified Level II technicians travel to your plant or yard with portable equipment, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the results.

faq.q: Can MT inspect aluminum transmission housings?
faq.a: No, aluminum is not ferromagnetic. Liquid penetrant testing is the surface method for aluminum, and the Indianapolis penetrant page explains how it works for housings and other non-magnetic parts.

faq.q: Is wet fluorescent MT better than dry powder?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles under UV-A light are the most sensitive and suit machined parts, but they need darkness. Dry powder suits rough, warm or outdoor welds. The procedure explains the selection.

faq.q: Why does the part need two examinations?
faq.a: Cracks show best when they cross the field. By magnetizing in two directions about ninety degrees apart, a crack in any orientation is found, as ASME Section V Article 7 requires.

faq.q: Does magnetism left in a part cause problems?
faq.a: It can. Residual magnetism can deflect a welding arc, attract chips into bearings or upset instruments, so the procedure states when demagnetization is required and how the residual field will be verified.

faq.q: Is a magnet inspection service the same as MT?
faq.a: No. Inspection of lifting magnets is covered by ASME B30.20 and belongs to the owner. MT is a crack-detection method used on hooks, pins, lugs and structures of lifting devices.

faq.q: What do I need to send for a quote?
faq.a: Send the part list or drawings, material, surface and coating condition, the acceptance code and edition, power and access details, and your target dates. Photographs of the weld areas help.

faq.q: Can Atlantis teach MT to my staff?
faq.a: Yes. Atlantis offers MT Level 1 and Level 2 training, and your company certifies its technicians under its own SNT-TC-1A written practice, since the employer issues the qualification.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Indianapolis, IN | LPT
pt.description: On-site liquid penetrant testing in Indianapolis for aluminum housings, stainless piping, castings and welds. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) and Dye Penetrant Inspection in Indianapolis, Indiana
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes liquid penetrant technicians to Indianapolis plants, machine shops, castings suppliers, food and pharmaceutical facilities and fabricators to find surface-breaking cracks, porosity and laps in aluminum, stainless steel, nickel alloys, brass and other non-magnetic metals, as well as in steel welds. Request a PT quote for your Indianapolis site with the material, surface condition and acceptance code, and we reply within one business day.

Where liquid penetrant testing is used in Indianapolis

Indianapolis is a drivetrain and engine town, and many of the parts that come out of its plants are not magnetic or cannot be tested with particles. Aluminum housings, cases and pistons, machined stainless fittings and nickel-alloy engine parts all need a surface check, and penetrant testing is the method that provides it. Foundries that pour aluminum and iron use PT to find shrinkage and surface porosity. Fabricators welding stainless steel check root and cap passes with dye penetrant, and maintenance teams use it to prove that a ground-out repair cavity has no crack remaining before it is welded again.

Indiana's food, beverage, ethanol and pharmaceutical plants rely on stainless steel vessels and piping, and a surface crack in a sanitary weld is both a leak path and a place for product to hide. Penetrant testing is a standard way to verify those welds during construction and repair.

  • Aluminum castings and machined housings: porosity, cold shuts, cracks at bosses and ports
  • Stainless steel and nickel alloy welds on process piping, tanks and vessels
  • Repair excavations on any alloy before re-welding
  • Brass, bronze and copper fittings, and titanium parts where the code allows penetrant

Atlantis does not run the aerospace fluorescent penetrant lines that some engine suppliers operate under customer process approvals.

What PT finds, and what it cannot

Penetrant testing finds discontinuities that are open to the surface. A thin liquid is drawn into the opening by capillary action, excess penetrant is removed from the surface, and a developer draws the trapped liquid back out to make a visible mark. The method can be used on ferrous and non-ferrous metals, ceramics and some plastics, provided the material is non-porous.

A flaw that is closed at the surface, whether by smeared metal, shot-blasting or peening, will not take up penetrant. Oil, paint and scale also block the opening. Porous materials hold penetrant and give a noisy background, and flaws below the surface are invisible. The method says how long a crack is on the surface, not how deep it goes.

Choosing the penetrant system

Visible penetrant, typically red under a white developer, is the common field and shop choice because it needs only normal lighting. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and is examined under UV-A light in a darkened area, which is why it is chosen for fine fatigue cracks in critical parts. Removal can be by solvent wipe, by water wash, or by a post-emulsification step, and developers can be dry powder or wet, with non-aqueous wet developer being the practical field product. Materials for nickel alloys and austenitic stainless steels should be low in sulfur and halogens, and the procedure records the batch.

Technique, step by step

The area is cleaned and dried. Penetrant is applied and allowed to dwell; the excess is removed without flushing the flaw; developer is applied in a thin even film; and indications are inspected after the development time under the specified light. ASME Section V Article 6 sets a standard temperature range of 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for the part and the penetrant materials. Beyond those limits a procedure has to be qualified at the temperature actually met in the field.

Indianapolis winters make that limit a real issue. Steel and aluminum in an unheated building or yard can sit well below 40 degrees for weeks, so parts are warmed, or a low-temperature procedure is qualified using a reference block with known cracks, before the work is accepted. Summer surface temperatures can also exceed 125 degrees in sun, and the same logic applies.

Codes and acceptance criteria

The method is governed by ASME Section V Article 6, and ASTM E165 for general industry, with ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 for process piping, and AWS D1.1 or D1.6 for structural and stainless welds. For castings and machined parts, the customer specification usually names the acceptance standard, often a class system that sets limits by size and type of indication. Under API 510, API 570 and API 653, the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection decisions, and Atlantis performs the penetrant examination and reports it.

Indiana and plant requirements

Indiana boilers and pressure vessels fall under the Boilers and Pressure Vessels Section of the Indiana Department of Homeland Security and the rules in 675 IAC 30, with operating permits and licensed inspectors. A penetrant examination of a repair weld is part of the repair record. Indiana's own workplace safety plan covers chemical handling and ventilation, and the solvent cleaners and aerosol developers used in penetrant testing are flammable, so work inside vessels or tanks needs hazard communication review, atmospheric testing and ignition control before it starts. Pharmaceutical and food plants usually require approval of every chemical that may touch product-contact surfaces.

Surface preparation and cleanliness

The cleaning step often decides the result. Oil and machining coolant are removed with solvent or a detergent wash, paint and scale are stripped, and weld flux and spatter are chipped and wire-brushed away. For aluminum castings and machined parts, abrasive blasting and heavy sanding can smear metal over a crack, so the procedure may require chemical etching before penetrant is applied. Parts are dried completely, because water or solvent trapped in a crack blocks the penetrant. The report notes any surface conditioning that was carried out.

Castings, porosity and leak paths

Aluminum and iron castings are common in Indiana plants, and penetrant testing is how foundries and machine shops find surface porosity, shrinkage, cold shuts and cracks before expensive machining or assembly. Cast surfaces are rough, so penetrant is held in the texture and background can be high. Cleaning, removal technique and a thin developer film matter, and the procedure may specify a more sensitive or fluorescent system. Machined sealing faces and port bores are examined for porosity that would create a leak path, and findings are compared against the customer's casting class or specification.

Reading indications

A crack usually appears as a sharp line that grows slowly as penetrant bleeds out; porosity as a cluster of dots; a lap as a smooth curved line. The technician examines the surface while developer is working and again at the end of the development time, and distinguishes relevant indications from lint, scratches and residue by wiping the spot clean and re-applying developer. Indication length, shape and spacing are measured and compared with the acceptance rules. Atlantis reports the facts and leaves repair and rework decisions to the owner and the inspector responsible under the governing code.

Repairs, re-examination and records

When a crack is found, the area is excavated by grinding, and penetrant is used again to prove the crack is gone before welding resumes. The finished repair is examined once more after the weld has cooled. Each repair is tracked with an identifier, so the report shows what was found, what was removed and what was accepted. Atlantis keeps the records for the owner in the format that fits the quality system of the plant.

Materials and equipment checks

The technician confirms that cleaner, penetrant and developer are compatible and in date, that fluorescent light meters are within calibration, and that a reference panel shows the system working when the procedure requires it. Aerosol cans, rags and solvent waste are handled under the site's hazardous waste rules. In tanks, vessels and other confined spaces, ventilation and atmospheric testing come first.

Who does the work

Penetrant testing is done by Level II technicians qualified under the company's written practice, based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with an ASNT Level III approving the procedure and reviewing reports. The employer issues the qualification. Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001.

What the PT report contains

The report records the component, location and drawing, the penetrant, remover and developer by type and batch, the cleaning and removal methods, dwell and development times, the surface and material temperature, the light intensity, and the technician and level. Each indication is logged with location, length and type, photographed where practical, and accepted or rejected against the named code. If post-cleaning was required, the report states how it was done, because residual penetrant on stainless steel and aluminum is itself a problem for some owners.

Planning a PT job in Indianapolis

Technicians travel to your site. Temperature and cleanliness shape the plan: cold plants need warmed parts or a qualified low-temperature procedure, humid summer days slow drying, and areas with floor drains, product exposure or food contact need cleanup and chemical approvals in advance. Outage windows at process plants, foundry pour schedules and fabricator delivery dates all need to be known before dates are set. Plant orientation and safety training take time. Atlantis has no office in Indianapolis, so the quote includes mobilization to your site.

PT, MT or UT for your Indianapolis job

Penetrant is the right method for aluminum, stainless and other non-magnetic material. On carbon steel and iron, magnetic particle inspection in Indianapolis is quicker and finds near-surface flaws too. When the question is thickness or internal weld quality, use ultrasonic testing in Indianapolis. The MT versus PT comparison, the Article 6 explainer, the Indiana inspection services hub and the national penetrant testing page provide more background.

Training your own PT technicians

Many shops start in-house NDT with penetrant testing. Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, plus the PT practical simulator, and the Indianapolis NDT training page has local detail. Your company certifies its technicians under its written practice.

faq.q: What can dye penetrant inspection check in Indianapolis?
faq.a: Any non-porous surface: aluminum housings and castings, stainless steel welds and fittings, nickel alloys, brass, and steel welds. It finds only flaws open to the surface, so internal conditions need ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep a team in Indianapolis for PT?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Indianapolis. Qualified technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, working under a written practice built on SNT-TC-1A with an ASNT Level III approving procedures.

faq.q: Can penetrant testing be done in an Indiana winter?
faq.a: Yes, if the part temperature is controlled. ASME Section V Article 6 sets 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, so cold parts are warmed or a low-temperature procedure is qualified with a reference block.

faq.q: What is the difference between visible and fluorescent penetrant?
faq.a: Visible penetrant is usually red on a white developer and needs normal light. Fluorescent penetrant glows under UV-A light, is more sensitive, and requires a darkened area to inspect.

faq.q: Does Atlantis run aerospace fluorescent penetrant lines?
faq.a: No. Aerospace lines run to customer process specifications and approvals that Atlantis does not hold. Atlantis penetrant work in Indianapolis is for industrial plants, fabricators, foundries and construction.

faq.q: Why can blasting or grinding hide cracks from penetrant?
faq.a: Abrasive work can smear metal across a crack opening, closing it so penetrant cannot enter. The procedure may call for chemical etching on aluminum and soft alloys before the penetrant is applied.

faq.q: Is penetrant safe to use on stainless steel and nickel alloys?
faq.a: Yes, with materials controlled for sulfur and halogens and with post-cleaning where required. The procedure records the batch and states what cleaning follows the examination.

faq.q: What do I send to get a PT quote?
faq.a: Send drawings or part lists, materials, surface condition, the code or customer specification, access conditions, the temperature range of the work area, and your target dates so the procedure and schedule can be matched to the job.

faq.q: Can Atlantis teach PT to my staff?
faq.a: Yes. Courses cover PT Level 1 and Level 2, and trainees can rehearse on a simulator. Your company then certifies its technicians under its written practice, because the employer issues the qualification under SNT-TC-1A.

rt.title: Radiography Alternatives: UT & Level III | Indianapolis, IN
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For Indianapolis, IN we offer UT where codes allow, plus ASNT Level III review of radiographs and procedures.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in Indianapolis, Indiana
rt.html:
Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing anywhere in the United States, including Indianapolis. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity under Nuclear Regulatory Commission rules in 10 CFR Part 34, or the equivalent rules of an Agreement State, and it is not a service Atlantis offers here. The sections below describe the alternatives available to an Indianapolis owner who searched for RT.

Why industrial radiography is licensed

Radiography exposes film or a detector with a gamma source or an X-ray tube. The companies and individuals who do it must hold a license or registration for the place where the work is carried out, must follow radiation safety rules and must clear work areas around the exposure. The licensing rules differ from state to state, so an owner in Indiana should confirm that any radiography contractor holds the authorization that applies at its site. Atlantis does not take on this work, and does not recommend or refer a particular radiography contractor.

Ultrasonic testing as a volumetric alternative

Where the construction code and the owner allow it, ultrasonic examination can take the place of radiography for weld quality. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII permits ultrasonic examination instead of radiography only under specific conditions. The substitution is never automatic. It must be agreed with the owner, the design engineer and, for code work, the authorized inspector before the job begins, and the agreement belongs in the procedure and quality plan. Where it exists, Atlantis technicians travel to your site for ultrasonic weld inspection in Indianapolis. Because no radiation boundary is needed, nearby trades can keep working, which matters in a busy plant or a shop with several crews.

ASNT Level III review of radiographs, with no radiation license

Judging radiographs does not require a radiation license, because no source is handled. An Atlantis ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. Typical requests from Indiana owners are a second read on disputed indications, a check that image quality indicators and density met the technique, and a review of an RT contractor's procedure and written practice. The founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. These reviews are done from the documents and images you send. See ASNT Level III consulting and written practice development for how such engagements are set up.

RT training theory

Technicians who want to understand radiographic interpretation can study through the radiographic testing Level 2 course. Source handling and the practical examination belong to a licensed employer, which then certifies its own personnel under a written practice based on SNT-TC-1A.

Other conventional methods in Indianapolis

For surface cracks, Atlantis performs magnetic particle inspection in Indianapolis on steel and iron and liquid penetrant testing in Indianapolis on aluminum, stainless and other non-magnetic metals. Atlantis has no office in Indianapolis, so technicians are mobilized to your site. Request a quote for ultrasonic work in Indianapolis with your drawings and the code your weld must meet, or see the NDT inspection services in Indiana hub.

faq.q: Is radiography available from Atlantis in Indianapolis?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not carry out radiography anywhere in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed. Atlantis offers ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant work, plus ASNT Level III review.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace RT on my Indiana weld job?
faq.a: Only if your construction code and owner allow it. ASME B31.3, API 1104, AWS D1.1 and ASME Section VIII each handle UT differently, so agree the substitution with the engineer and inspector first.

faq.q: Can Atlantis review radiographs from another contractor?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the code, and give a second opinion on disputed indications without any radiation license.

faq.q: Where can my team learn radiographic interpretation theory?
faq.a: Through the radiographic testing Level 2 course from Atlantis for theory. Source handling and practical examination are done by a licensed employer that certifies its own staff under SNT-TC-1A.

faq.q: Does Atlantis recommend an RT contractor near Indianapolis?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not name or recommend radiography contractors. We can review the procedure and images you already hold, or provide ultrasonic, magnetic particle and penetrant inspection.
